utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted and Thomas Laugel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The record should reflect that we sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis, Judge Mindua being absent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, the usher is going to hand back to you your two written statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could have 1D2318, tab 261, back on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, yesterday you testified that it was Miroslav Vasic who read back to you in Serbian your January 1998 statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If you could take a look at your January 1998 statement, I want to draw your attention to the last page of that statement where you'll find a certification by the interpreter employed by the ICTY and approved by the ICTY Registry certifying that she "orally translated the above statement from English language to Serbian language in the presence of Vojin Susa (and all other persons indicated on the first page of this statement) who appeared to have heard and understood my translation of this Statement." Then we see under item 4, the interpreter certifies that: "Vojin Susa has acknowledged that the facts and matters set out in his Statement, as translated by me, are true to the best of his knowledge and recollection ..." And then we can see on the original that the interpreter signed the certification and dated it. Mr. Susa, it was the ICTY interpreter who read to you this statement in the Serbian language, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Successively, as the conversation went on, she interpreted things to me. At the end she did not take any document, written, from beginning to end, to read it out to me again. I confirm hereby that during the taking of the interview she interpreted everything to me correctly. At that time I wasn't able to know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But this certification doesn't pertain to the interview. It pertains to the written statement, Mr. Susa. Is it your position that what is certified here is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To some extent, at the end of the day, it's not correct. This statement that I read the statement in Serbian and confirmed that it's correct is not true. The interpreter did not have a text in front of her to read back to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to confirm, we see in the first page that a representative of the Office of the Prosecution, Mr. Stefan Waespi was also present when your statement was read back to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry for my intervention, but I didn't see that Stefan Waespi was present when the statement was read back to the witness. I cannot see it in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's on the first page. It lists all persons present, and it specifies when that person was present only on one of the days. And we see that Stefan Waespi is listed as a last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not object -- [Microphone not activated] I did not object because Stefan Waespi was not present to do interview but to read back the statement to the witness. It was not in the statement. Or I cannot see the reference about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't believe that's a valid objection. I can put to this witness that Mr. Waespi was present when the statement was read back to him, and that is what we believe was indicated on the front page of this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, Mr. Waespi was also present when your statement was read back to you, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I contend that this statement was not read back to me. I cannot tell you who was in the room at that moment. There were several people. I don't know Mr. Waespi. He must be one of the investigators of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The person who interviewed you for the statement, that person was there when you signed the statement after it was read back to you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. I cannot really tell you who was there when the end of the statement was put to me. But I repeat emphatically, the entire statement in English was not read back to me. As I was talking, everything was interpreted, both my words and what people said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have P2518, this is tab 1, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, I'm now going to return to the SFRY Law on Military Courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention again to Article 9, which we were talking about at the end of the day yesterday. And you'll recall that you testified that a member of the Territorial Defence could possibly qualify as military personnel under this Article 9 as a civilian carrying out specific military duties. Now, first of all, I agree with you that a member of the Territorial Defence was a civilian under SFRY laws regulating the military, but would you allow for the possibility that "specific military duties" refers to civilians who are under a fixed-term contract to perform certain duties for the military, such as a barber or an auto mechanic?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday you noted quite correctly that I am no expert for this Law on the Army. I encountered it only rarely, perhaps when I was taking an exam at law school. You're asking me now to interpret legal provisions that I am not familiar with. Then allow me to say that a much broader range of people are covered by this provision, not only the barber, the baker, and such in the army. They are not the military. I believe they are commonly referred to as civilians serving in the army, in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The SBWS Territorial Defence, which you described, I believe, yesterday or the day before, as a disjointed village guard system, was not part of the SFRY armed forces and that is why the SBWS Grand National Assembly issued its 9 October 1991 decision seeking to place the Territorial Defence within the SFRY armed forces; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. You mentioned several stages. At the outset, indeed, we had only village guards. Those village guards, with the arrival of Radovan Stojicic, Badza, were integrated, united into the Territorial Defence of SBWS. That Territorial Defence was later resubordinated to JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified -- well, you just mentioned Radovan Stojicic. He was a member of the Serbian MUP. He wasn't a member of the army. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but at that moment, at that stage, there were intertwined jurisdictions that we didn't know. We didn't know what arrangements were made between the MUP and the army as to what they would be doing on the ground. We accepted them as forces that came from the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I take it from your last answer that you never inquired about this issue, about jurisdiction, with either the military or the police? You just assumed that one of them had jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that both of them have jurisdiction, but we didn't know how their competencies were divided.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss the issue of jurisdiction with the Serbian MUP or the JNA command?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We believed we were not qualified for that and there was no need for that because we felt, still, and it was indeed so, in fact, as a part of the territory of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 2 of this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Mr. Susa, I appreciate what you said about not being an expert on military law, but I'll try to keep my questions general so that you'll be able to follow along. I want you to look at Article 13 which enumerates the instances when the military courts exercise jurisdiction over civilians and other persons who do not fall within the definition of military personnel. And if you look at the crimes listed under paragraph 1, we see ten on this page, these crimes were either crimes against the state or crimes against the military under chapters 15 and chapters 20 of the SFRY criminal code; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I allow for that possibility. I can now not speak to the exact meaning of every law. I cannot reproduce it correctly now. I would have to refresh my memory. It's mainly because this law has not been in force for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I understand that. And we have the SFRY criminal code into evidence, and I won't turn to that for now but I'll accept your answer. Now, under this law, the military courts had exclusive jurisdiction over these crimes regardless of whether they are committed by civilian or military personnel; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The remaining paragraphs of Article 13 describe other circumstances in which the military courts exercised jurisdiction over persons who are not military personnel. And I want to draw your attention in particular to the last paragraph, paragraph 4, of Article 13, which gives the military courts jurisdiction over prisoners of war for war crimes under chapter 16 of the SFRY criminal code. In the context of the conflict in the SBWS, this meant that Croat prisoners of war fell within the exclusive jurisdiction of the military courts; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could look at Article 15, which I think is still on the same page but a little lower.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that if a serviceman and a civilian commit a criminal offence as co-perpetrators or as accomplices and if the civilian's crimes fall within the jurisdiction of a regular court, that regular court also tries the serviceman, the exception being crimes falling under paragraph 4 relating to prisoners of war. Mr. Susa, this meant that the civilian courts had jurisdiction over crimes committed jointly by civilian and military personnel which did not fall within Article 13; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conclude from Article 15, paragraph 1, that that could be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could look at Article 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If the accused's military status has ceased by the day of the confirmation of the indictment and if the criminal offence did not fall under Article 13, paragraphs 1 and 2, the regular court had jurisdiction over the case, and this meant that non-Article 13 crimes committed by a soldier who ceased to be a member of the army before he was indicted fell within the competency of the civilian courts; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and jurisdiction fell to the court that instigated the proceedings. It had to declare itself competent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you testified yesterday that the SBWS judiciary's jurisdiction over crimes was narrowed down considerably because the army had powers, according to legislation, that governed immediate threat of war. What were the laws you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I meant this law and special provisions relating to the state of imminent threat of war, which is almost the same as the state of war. I believe in that situation, all these provisions have a different meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, now I've looked through this legislation and I haven't seen any provisions regarding expansion of the jurisdiction under immediate threat of war. Can you point to any other legislation that governs or expands the military court's jurisdiction in the case of immediate threat of war?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, at this moment I don't know anything about the operation of such laws. All I know that all crimes that were perpetrated on the ground were handled by military prosecutors and military courts. If there was a problem, they were duty-bound to declare themselves not competent and cede the cases to us, but they didn't do that. They may have thought that we were still not organised well enough. That's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at a few examples of the application of this SFRY Law on Military Courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have on the screen 65 ter 6677, this is tab 165.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I believe you had a chance to look at this document during proofing. It is a 11 June 1992 motion from the military investigative judge to the Belgrade military court, and the motion pertains to the case against Dusan Boljevic and Jagoda Boljevic which you mentioned yesterday during your testimony. Now, you were aware that Dusan Boljevic was a member of the Baranja TO when he committed war crimes against Croat civilians; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that and it was not my duty to know that. It was up to the agencies that handled specific actions regarding these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned in your 2014 statement that the Beli Manastir SUP submitted a criminal report against Boljevic to the military prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the civilian police had the obligation, didn't they, to report crimes regardless of whether they believed the perpetrator was a civilian or a military personnel; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case that's what they did. Of course, they had to investigate the crime scene and collect evidence about the possible suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that wasn't quite my question. My question is: It was their duty, their obligation, if they learned about a crime, they have to report it to the appropriate authorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what I confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, on paragraph 1, we see that the military court classified Mr. Boljevic as a civilian. And if we look at paragraph 2, the investigative judge notes that prior -- notes the prior dismissal of the charge of theft of military equipment. Now, that would have been a crime against the military which would have fallen under Article 13 of the Law on Military Courts; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must warn you that this is the final document. The beginning of the case against the Boljevics was for a much more serious crime; and that is to say, multiple murder. This passage is not reflective of the entirety. In the investigation, he was charged with much more serious crimes. If it had not been that way ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I'll get to that. Thank you, Mr. Susa. But just focusing on this more minor crime of theft of military equipment, that was a crime against the military and therefore the military courts had exclusive jurisdiction over that; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over this? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Then if we continue in the second paragraph, the investigative judge concludes that because the remaining charges - and those charges would have included, as you were suggesting, the war crimes charges, the murder charges - do not belong to the group of criminal offences that fall under the jurisdiction of the military court regarding civilians, which are stated in Article 13 of the Law on Military Courts. And based on that, he concludes that the military court no longer has jurisdiction over this case. That was a correct application of the law we looked at, isn't it, Mr. Susa?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be correct even if it had been applied much earlier, not 11 June 1992, when they returned this case to us but on a grounds that, according to my opinion, was not lawful. They should have taken over this case in order to investigate much more serious crimes. In any case, we accepted this case and we tried Boljevic. We did not cause any conflict of jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted to evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 6677 will be Exhibit P3275.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could now have on the screen 65 ter 6679, this is tab 167.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Susa, you had an opportunity to look at this during proofing. This is a 20 April 1992 decision by the Belgrade military court. Now, we can see that this decision was issued a month before the immediate threat of war was terminated in the SFRY; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could look at the first paragraph and then into the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that the decision dismisses the case against Mile Stevanovic and Dragan Jocevic [phoen] for the crimes of aggravated theft and murder committed while members of the volunteer detachment Leva Supoderica from TO Vukovar. And they dismiss it based on lack of subject matter jurisdiction. First of all, were you aware of this case?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as you can see, he ended up in the -- or this ended up in the district court in Belgrade via the military investigative organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But I understand that you are not familiar with this particular case?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if we look at page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I think for you it's paragraphs 3 and 4. We see the reasons provided for the dismissal is that the status of Stevanovic, as a serviceman, was terminated before the indictment became legally valid, and because the criminal offence did not fall within Article 13, the court lacked jurisdiction over him under Article 16 of the Law on Military Courts. Now, we can also see with regard to the other accused, because at least one of the co-perpetrators was not military personnel, the case was terminated under Article 15 of the Law on Military Courts. Mr. Susa, this is a correct application of Articles 15 and 16 of the Law on Military Courts that we just looked at a moment ago, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would really need to look at this in more detail but I don't want to insist because of the time. Let us say that this is correct but perhaps there are some details of dispute in all of this. I think that at the time of the commission of the crime, the person had the status of a military serviceman. Once the status was terminated, I cannot really say whether he immediately fell under the jurisdiction of the civilian authorities. In order to say anything about that, I would really need to look at the law. In any event, this case was not under our jurisdiction, before or after, and I really don't know anything more about the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, we tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 6679 will be Exhibit P3276.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let us look at one more of these decisions, 65 ter 6680, this is tab 168.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, sir, you may be familiar with this particular case because, as I understand it, it did make its way back to the SBWS courts or RSK courts. This is a 22 May 1992 letter from the Belgrade military court regarding the case against Risto Buha and others who were members of the Jankovci Territorial Defence. Were you familiar with this case back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of the whole event. It's particularly painful to me. I'm also familiar with the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, the president of the military court in Belgrade informs the SBWS court in Vukovar that it had determined that it lacked subject matter jurisdiction in this case on 31 March 1992. Now, this is nearly two months before the immediate threat of war was rendered null and void in SFRY; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just a decision on the 31 March 1992 and the date of the document is the 22nd of May, 1992. The 31st of March, 1992, is the final date when the decision goes into effect under number 218/92. I am aware of the case. It's painful because it is about the death or killing of friends of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You're aware that Risto Buha and the other perpetrators in this case were acquitted and acquitted by the RSK courts?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I was tragically surprised when I saw that while preparing for this case, this testimony, and when I saw why this happened. I actually didn't know anything about this until one or two months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 6680 will be Exhibit P3277.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, the decisions we've just looked at demonstrate that the end of the state of imminent threat of war in SFRY had no impact on the jurisdiction of the military courts. Rather, what did have an impact was whether the perpetrator was a member of the JNA at the time of the offence as well as at the time of the indictment; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is only true to an extent. A large number of cases were handed over only after the imminent threat of war was rendered null and void. You cited examples which indicate that this was done in this manner as well, but that wasn't the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let us look at 65 ter 6672. This is tab 163.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a bit difficult to read, Mr. Susa, but I'll try to assist you.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What this is is a collection of case file documents in a case against Momcilo Vekic. Do you know who Momcilo Vekic was?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, pages 1 and 2 are a 10 March 1992 criminal report filed by the Vukovar SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the case involved the theft of a large quantity of corn from the Ludvinci village in February 1992. Ludvinci is near Bobota, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say. I don't really know that area very well. Maybe it's a small hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we turn to page -- the next page, page 3 in the English -- actually, if we could stay on page 2 for the original. Page 3 for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We can see that Momcilo Vekic was commander of the TO staff in Ludvinci. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me just for one moment, please. Could you please just show me which paragraph that was? That would make it easier for me to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. Let me see if I can help you. I don't -- I have it marked in the English.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would that not be among the general information on the first page?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No, no, it's a -- thank you for the suggestion, but it's -- it's -- it would be -- is it the last paragraph or the penultimate paragraph on this page? Actually -- yes, the last paragraph at the very bottom. It says: "Since the reported person, Momcilo Vekic, is the commander of the TO staff in Ludvinci ..." And it continues from there. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Now I see it. But it's -- all right. Very well. I have read it, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 16 now in both the original and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that the RSK prosecutor dismissed this case in April 1992. Now, he's not dismissing it due to lack of subject matter jurisdiction but because the accused harvested the corn with the knowledge and approval of the TO staff. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it but I believe that what you have read is true, so there is no need for me to look at it. I do see the statement of reasons and the part where it says that the report is being dismissed. And even though it's illegible, I accept that what you read is correct. It's very, very difficult to read the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, and I apologise for that. But the point being is this is an instance where the SBWS police and the judiciary investigated and initiated proceedings against a commander of a local TO unit; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 6672 will be Exhibit P3278.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, it was the case, wasn't it, that with only a few exceptions, the JNA military courts did not initiate prosecutions of local Serbs in SBWS for crimes committed against non-Serb civilians or hors de combat?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. That assertion is a very general one and it does not correspond to the truth. Perhaps sometimes it happened, but according to what I know, in most cases this does not apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you give us an estimate of how many cases the military courts pursued against Serb perpetrators from SBWS for crimes committed against non-Serbs? Can you give us your figure on that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, that would just be a very approximate generalisation. But this information would have been in the possession of officials who prosecuted these crimes. They would have all of those statistics and the precise figures. We in the ministry did not deal with things like that. I could give you a rough estimate, but it would just be guessing and I don't want to make up any data that I'm not sure of.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Fair enough. But let me ask you this: We've talked about the Boljevic case and we've talked about the Buha case. Can you identify any other cases of Serb perpetrators from the SBWS who committed crimes against non-Serbs in the SBWS that were pursued by the military court? And by "pursued," I mean they actually prosecuted it.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You think that originally they were under the jurisdiction of the military court and then later they were returned to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. You -- you are representing to us that a large number of these cases came to the RSK judiciary sometime in the early summer of 1992, and I'm asking you: Can you identify any other cases other than the Buha case and the Boljevic case?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood partially what I said. When I said a large number of cases were returned to us, I did not say that that was a large number of cases with Serbs committing crimes against ethnic Croats. I simply spoke about a large number of cases. In that structure, I again note I don't know how many cases were of this nature. It's something that I didn't need to know. This is something that officials of basic, district, and regional courts would know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But you were aware that the JNA wasn't performing its law enforcement duties properly and in fact JNA officers were engaged in looting and, I believe you testified yesterday, in the expulsion of non-Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can speak about this in general terms, but I don't have specific evidence about the conduct of individuals. That is something that I could not have had. I am just talking about the results of the work of certain organs which reported their work through reports, but I don't have the specific reports to be able to give my comments on them. Yes, there were cases in the field when everybody, including JNA officers, committed abuses; specifically, when I come to that or I can say that already now, I can give you those examples. Unfortunately, those cases, those examples were never prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Mr. Susa, that's precisely my point. You were aware that the JNA itself was -- members of the JNA itself were committed the crimes and yet they weren't being prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not talking about crimes. I was talking about abuses, misdemeanors. First of all, talking about Ilok where a large number of material goods were exported. There was no evidence there of any crimes being committed. Perhaps this was transferred to another location under the control of some other organs. Crimes and this, in my view, are completely different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But you'll agree that expulsions are serious crimes?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, expulsions are a serious crime. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified earlier this week that you attended a meeting in Dalj at the town library, and I think you mentioned it was in August of 1991. That meeting was held on the 18th of August, 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an informal meeting. It was not an official meeting, but yes, that would be the correct day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this town library where the meeting was held, that was Goran Hadzic's government office in Dalj; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that point in time, we didn't actually have any government offices. The government hadn't even been formed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But that -- that building became Mr. Hadzic's office in Dalj, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend any government meetings at that office in Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Zivanovic, I did not hear what you stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the previous question, "And this town library where the meeting was held, that was Goran Hadzic's government office in Dalj?" Answer: "No." "But that building became Mr. Hadzic's office in Dalj, didn't it?"

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I don't understand. But anyway, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, at this informal meeting, Mr. Hadzic appointed you minister of justice as well as appointed Slavko Dokmanovic and others present to their posts in what would become the future government; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not me. Definitely not. What was discussed at the meeting was who in future would be able to perform any function. The function of Slavko Dokmanovic on that day was very controversial. A large number of people were against him because of his conduct in Vukovar when he was the mayor. Here we were just dealing with different matters and how and whether we would be working in certain ways in the future, but nobody was appointed to any posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If you could take a look at your January 1998 statement, and if you could turn to paragraph 12 of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In the English it's on page 5, I don't know what it is on the Serbian version. But it's paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The first sentence reads: "Mr. Dokmanovic was also appointed with me. I think it was on 18 August 1991 in Dalj." That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would just like to note here that you could not present this quite like this time-wise. You can treat it however you want but we were appointed as members of the government at the assembly. These were just things that later did not have to materialise, and then later we did not even function as a government until after the assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So your position is until the 25th of September, 1991, there was in effect no government in SBWS?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely clear. It could not have existed until it was confirmed at the assembly. The assembly elects the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now besides appointments, what else was discussed at this 18 August meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting of the 18th of August did not function in the way that somebody would speak and everybody else would listen to them. There was a large number of people there who were talking in groups, precisely because they were preparing for something that was waiting for them in the future. I spent the entire meeting in talks with judges from Vukovar, Mr. Vojnovic, Stankovic, perhaps Mr. Jovan Ajdukovic was there as well. We were standing in a corner and we were talking about our own tasks that were ahead of us. There was a group over there among whom I saw Radovan Stojicic, Badza. Later I found out who that was. I think that Mr. Hadzic was in some sort of side room and he was also talking with somebody. At no point during that meeting nothing happened that would, I repeat, mean that everybody was listening to a single speaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified that prior to this meeting, that you had met Goran Hadzic once at the home foundation in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was that the association of Serbs from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is officially the home association of Serbs, and it is -- it's based in Belgrade. And emigres from all parts of the world would come to that association.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And at that time who was the head of that association?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Brana Crncevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us, was this meeting in July 1991 or this gathering that you saw Mr. Hadzic at?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not really a meeting. We just saw each other in passing. He didn't come because of me and I wasn't there because of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was it in July?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I cannot really be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In paragraph 26 of your 2014 statement, you state that at the invitation of Milos Vojnovic, you became engaged in the establishment of the civilian government in SBWS under Serbian control. You further state that several other colleagues joined you "with whom we had daily meetings." This is -- sir, this is your 2014 statement.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the paragraph number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Certainly. It's paragraph 26. And you state again, I'll repeat, that at the invitation of Milos Vojnovic, you became engaged in the establishment of the civilian government in SBWS under Serbian control, and you further state that several other colleagues joined you with whom you had daily meetings. And my first question to you is: When did these daily meetings take place?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back since the beginning of July -- no, in fact, in July 1991, I was still in Vinkovci. It should be sometime in the beginning of August when they visited me in the apartment where I was recovering.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who participated in these daily meetings?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not daily meetings. They would just come to discuss our future work in the Ministry of Justice. Mr. Kovacevic, Jovan Ajdukovic. I'm not sure about Sremac. Maybe I mentioned him, too. And I believe there were one or two colleagues whom I didn't know until then. With these people whom I knew before, I remembered them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And at the end of paragraph it states that at one of these meetings, which now you're saying weren't daily but nevertheless they occurred, the attendees told you that Goran Hadzic, who had a mandate to form the government, had great faith in you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. We knew each other from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, as SBWS minister of justice, you had one deputy minister and three assistant ministers who reported to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you give us their names?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovan Ajdukovic, Sinisa Puskar, Vojo Ore. They were not the same people all the time. They rotated. Nenad Stankovic. I can't remember them all. There were a number of people within a short period. Stevo Pulic got involved later as the man who enforced criminal sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll ask you to put your statement away for now, and I want to turn your attention to L1.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is tab 31. And this is the Official Gazette for SBWS. And if we could turn to page 63 of the English, page 21 of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I believe you testified that judges and prosecutors were appointed by the SBWS Grand National Assembly in October of 1991, and we see here a list of those who were appointed. With the exception of Bela Bolsek [phoen] in Beli Manastir, they're all Serbs, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this reflected the policy of both the SBWS and RSK governments to appoint Serbs to positions within the judiciary, isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not the case. We would have gladly taken advantage of the knowledge of our colleagues who were Serbs [as interpreted], but unfortunately there were none. One of my ministers later at the ministry was a lady who was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic. I see it as well. Non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is a problem in transcript with the translation. In line -- in line third, page 25. It is said that: "We would have gladly taken advantage of the knowledge of our colleagues who were Serbs, but unfortunately" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And the witness said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who were not Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. It's on the record now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You said that you had a minister who was a woman, Croat? What was her official title?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was my deputy in charge of administration. For a while she was the secretary of the Ministry of Justice while she was in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, we can see from this decision that Milos Vojnovic was appointed president of the SBWS Supreme Court based in Vukovar. Now, as supreme court president, he supervised the work of the courts and he also issued legal opinions to the courts; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to 1D1008. This is tab 232.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We can see that he was also your assistant.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. If you mean that because of the fact he was made president of the district court his role in the ministry should have been cancelled, we couldn't do that. We had a shortage of personnel. And later he became exclusively president of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D1008 will be Exhibit P3279.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Once the SBWS judiciary began functioning at the beginning of November 1991, the focus of its work was on investigating and prosecuting crimes committed by non-Serbs, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite the contrary. We focused very quickly on daily life and the crimes in daily life were mostly committed by Serbs, and I would not say that we had already established a system. Those were only the beginning. We were still very far from being fully operative as the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let us look at P3228.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have again a problem in the translation. The witness did not say: "We were still very far from being fully operative as the Ministry of Justice." He -- he used another term.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, did you hear that? Could you correct, if necessary?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mean my ministry. I meant the judiciary system as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have P3228 on the screen. This is tab 187.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a 10 December 1991 memorandum from the district public prosecute to the SBWS government. Mr. Cosic reports that the public prosecutor's office started working effectively at the beginning of November 1991, and he then writes: "Presently, it is mostly working on identify and prosecuting Ustasha criminals, the protection of property primarily in Vukovar but also in the entire district. Today we have received over 70 criminal reports and we have processed most of them. And it is therefore realistic to expect that the first trials will open soon before the courts of the Serbian District." He then writes: "As our work is not static and tied to one location ..." And then he requests additional fuel and vehicles. Now, first of all, the judiciary was carrying out investigations and prosecutions in the entire district as reported by Mr. Trosic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They prosecuted in the entire territory of the Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. In fact, they acted upon the criminal complaints filed by the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the judiciary was mostly working on identifying and prosecuting Ustasha criminals because that was the priority advanced by the SBWS government, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Definitely not. It was not any priority of the government. But Trosic [Realtime transcript read in error "Cosic"] as the district prosecutor could in a way direct the work of the prosecutor's office. They did collect a lot of information about crimes perpetrated, but there were no clear perpetrators. They had nothing to do. It was a strategy of the prosecutor's office that I had nothing to do with. They were doing it independently. But in operative daily terms, proceedings were taken against Serbs and they were in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I will just say that the name, Mr. Cosic, is not correct in the transcript. It is in line 22 of page 27 and in line 6 of page 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's correct, it's Mr. Trosic, we are talking about, T-r-o-s-i-c.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again it's not good. It's T-r-o-s-i-c, Trosic. Now it's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, and please excuse my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could play a video now. This is 65 ter 4882.1. This is tab 113. And I believe the interpreters have the transcript in both English and in B/C/S. Okay. If we can begin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The Croatian Television ... echoing Franjo Tudjman and the Croatian leadership's call to the Croatians to return to the places they had left, is yet another attempt by Tudjman and the Croatian leaders to show their well-known cynicism, meaning that they want to let the European public know, actually, they want to reverse the thesis about a people's exodus and depict the Croatians as the ones who are being purged, when we, Serbians, know that it is not true. I want to say that Franjo Tudjman's statement in his own personal affair -- is his own personal affair, and that one cannot implement the Croatian government and the Croatian authorities' jurisdiction in our territory. We are a Serbian region, where the Serbians have explicitly chosen to live in a single federal unit, a single federal community, together with any other nation wishing to remain in Yugoslavia, and here we implement our own regulations and laws, not the laws prescribed by the Croatian government. "Do you have a record of how many and which specific Croatians have compromised themselves? "So far we have no records about this. However, we know that a majority of the Croatians in our Serbian territories have compromised themselves and have actively co-operated with the Ustashe, and we shall try them for their crimes. Therefore, they can return, but they will be put through a regular court procedure. However, there are substantial numbers of those who have not compromised themselves. These are mostly people who never even left these territories. They continue to live in peace with their Serbian neighbours and other people."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Rade Leskovac, he was deputy SBWS minister of information and he's the one giving this interview; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I don't know if he was the deputy or an assistant of Mr. Ilija Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when asked about the number of Croats who had compromised themselves, he responded that: "... a majority of the Croatians in our Serbian territories have compromised themselves and have actively co-operated with the Ustashe, and we shall try them for their crimes." That was the official position of the SBWS government, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not quite sure about that. I believe that is his personal view. Whether it's a majority or a minority, we never made any official declarations. Nobody could have known it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the video will be Exhibit P3280 [Realtime transcript read in error "P2380"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we may have on the screen 1D846. This is tab 190.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't know -- ah, no. I don't know if the number of exhibit is correctly transcribed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number should be P3280. Thank you to counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have in front of us, Mr. Susa, is a 21 November 1991 memorandum from the district public prosecutor, again Mr. Trosic, to the SBWS Ministry of Interior and all SBWS courts. And Mr. Trosic requests all case files, documents, and evidence testifying to the genocide against the Serbian people and instructing that all accused and witnesses be questioned with regard to the genocide against the Serbian people without fail. Now, here again this reflects the priority of the judiciary was to prosecute non-Serbs for crimes against Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This doesn't come even close to prosecutions yet. It was one of the segments of the prosecutor's office. Certainly not the first thing on the list and not the decisive one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But it's clear from this letter it was a priority of the judiciary, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this letter it's evident that it's one of the tasks of this body, but I can't see from a single sentence that it's a priority. It's certainly one of the affairs they're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The SBWS and RSK courts only charged non-Serbs with the crime of genocide; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know we issued any indictments for genocide. I believe we issued more indictments against Serbs for crimes against Croats than vice versa. Maybe this indictment is correct [as interpreted]. We'll have to check that with the competent bodies. But you cannot say in any case that we only indicted Croats for crimes against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That wasn't my question and perhaps it wasn't translated properly. My question is with regard to the crime of genocide. And with regard to the crime of genocide, only non-Serbs were investigated or prosecuted for that particular crime. Serbs were never prosecuted for genocide by the SBWS or RSK courts; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Again, I don't know if the witness -- if it is correct. I didn't listen that -- it is in line 17: "Maybe this indictment is correct." I don't know what -- I don't believe that the witness said it and I don't know what indictment is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm re-asking my question because he really didn't answer it in the first case. And so if I could just ask again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, I asked my question to you a second time and it -- I'm only referring to the crime of genocide.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. Speaking of the crime of genocide, I don't believe there was a single investigation for that crime. You will correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, we'll come back to that. Now, in -- you mentioned in paragraph 153 of your 2014 statement - and you don't need to look at it unless you need to refresh your memory - but you state that the first war crimes trial in RSK was conducted in the Beli Manastir court against Dusan Boljevic. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. Maybe there was something before that, but I know about this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And he was convicted in 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you're not able to name a number -- another Serb who was prosecuted for war crimes by the SBWS or RSK courts, are you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had worked on it, I would have that information. Nobody told me that it was important. But I remembered this case because it's the most drastic one, the most impressive one. I am not qualified, really, to make a judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified this week that the RSK criminal code abolished the death penalty for general crimes. However, under the SFRY criminal code, which continued to apply in the RSK, genocide and war crimes remained punishable by death; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we do not have any powers to change federal laws. We were only qualified to change our laws and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The RSK courts continued to apply the SFRY criminal code well into 1992, 1993, until the SFRY criminal code itself was repealed subsequently; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you know how systems in the SFRY operated. Every republic had its own criminal code, and common crimes were covered by the federal law. The federal law did not govern special crimes. It was done by republican laws. The federal law contained the Federal Law on Criminal Procedure. That was common to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But my question was very specific: The RSK courts continued to apply the SFRY criminal code in 1992 and 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the procedural aspect they applied the Law on Criminal Procedure. As for specific qualifications of crimes and sanctions, they applied the Criminal Code of the Republic of Serbia and that was the first law that we changed and replaced by our own law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have 1D1029 on the screen. This is tab 141 -- I'm sorry, 241. And I think I could finish this document before the break. And if we could turn to page 2, the first page is just a cover letter or a file cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we see this is an 11 December 1991 memorandum from the district prosecutor Trosic to investigating judge of the Vukovar lower court. And in this, Mr. Trosic notes that the JNA identification commission filed a number of criminal reports against Ustasha criminals for the crime of genocide against the Serbian people and requests the report -- the court urgently to start interviewing witnesses regarding these crimes. Mr. Susa, this is yet another example of the SBWS judiciary implementing the priority of investigating war crimes committed against the Serb population; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is a tragic proof that victims of Croat crimes had already been identified, so it needed urgent action as soon as possible in order to be able to obtain evidence. So here we already have specific victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted to evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D1029 will be Exhibit P3281.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, I think, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is it an appropriate time, Mr. Olmsted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This would be an appropriate time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Susa, we take our first break, 30 minutes. We'll be back at 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, before the break we were talking about genocide investigations, and I would like to show you a couple examples of such investigations that the SBWS judiciary conducted in late 1991 and early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could 1D977 on the screen. This is tab 220.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a 9 December 1991 request to open an investigation, and the case is against Josip Horvat and two other Croats of -- charging them with committing genocide against a number of Serbs in September and October 1991 in Luzac. Now, this is an example of an investigation that was conducted into alleged charge of genocide against Serb victims, isn't it correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please show me the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is an investigation for the crime of genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could pull up 1D1102. This is tab 251.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that this is a recommendation for investigation issued by the Vukovar district public prosecutor's office to the Vukovar lower court. And under item 3 -- or first I should say this relates to the same case that we were looking at a moment ago. And under item 3, it states: "Issue a warrant for the arrest for the first accused, Josip Horvat, at the Collection Centre in Sremska Mitrovica and take him into custody to the Vukovar Court with temporary seat in Dalj." Mr. Horvat was one of the Sremska Mitrovica KP Dom detainees, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. It's quite possible, but I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified regarding this list of 20 to 30 Croats who were suspected of committing war crimes that the investigative judge has had with them when they went to Sremska Mitrovica prison was -- you can't say that his name was on that list?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any of the names from the list, and I don't know if I was ever shown this. These people were people I really didn't know at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we tender into evidence 1D977 and this 1D1102.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D977 will be Exhibit P3282. And 1D1102 will be Exhibit P3283.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could have on the screen 1D999. This is tab 224.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is a 13 January 1992 criminal report, which was issued by the district public prosecutor's office in Vukovar. And it charges Nikola Ivankovic and four other Croats with committing genocide in December 1991 in Paulin Dvor against 16 Serbs and a Hungarian. Mr. Susa, this is another example of a war crimes case that was prosecuted by the SBWS courts; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evidently.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D999 will be Exhibit P3284.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have on the screen P3262. This is tab 256.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Mr. Susa, what's going to appear on the screen is your 27 November 1991 letter that you wrote to the commander of the 1st Military District which you testified about earlier this week. And if you could take a look at the third paragraph, you write, with regard to the Croat prisoners of war held at Sremska Mitrovica KP Dom: "It is certain that in subsequent legal proceedings all persons who committed crimes against the armed forces will be under the jurisdiction of the military courts." Now that, Mr. Susa, is consistent with Article 13 of the Law on Military Courts that we looked at at the beginning of today as crimes against the armed forces falling under chapter 20 within the SFRY criminal code were within the exclusive jurisdiction of the military courts; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You then state: "But it is equally certain that persons who have committed crimes against the civilian population will have to be tried by the civilian courts that have subject matter and territorial jurisdiction, namely the ones that already exist and function in the Serbian District." It was your position and the position of the SBWS government that Croat prisoners of war from Vukovar and elsewhere who allegedly committed war crimes against the civilian population had to be tried in the SBWS by the SBWS courts; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my position. That was my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It was not only your position but it was the position of the government.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that most of the members of government didn't really understand this that well, but I allow that that was the position of the government. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that was the position of Mr. Hadzic, Goran Hadzic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this was your position even though, under Article 13 of the SFRY Law on Military Courts, the military courts had exclusive jurisdiction over these prisoners of war; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be so had we been sure that these were prisoners of war, but at the time of the commission of the crime we were not aware of what they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's look at your 2014 statement. If we could look at paragraph 105 of your recent statement. And in this paragraph you are providing evidence about the meeting at Velepromet on the 20th of November, 1991, and you begin by stating that you were informed at this meeting about the transfer of prisoners of war during the course of the day to various places in Serbia, including Sremska Mitrovica, somewhere near Nis, and Zrenjanin. And then you state, and I will quote you: "I would like to make it clear that we, the civilian authorities, did not make any decisions about where they would be taken and how these prisoners of war would be treated. In this initial phase, but also later, the military authorities alone were responsible for questions relating to prisoners of war." You use the word "prisoners of war," and I put to you that you knew that they were prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the point in time when they were treated as prisoners of war, nobody could have known. At the time when investigations were being carried out into the crimes, perhaps they were not even supposed to be in uniform. This is something that would have been established by the investigation. Now they were in the group of prisoners of war, but that does not mean that they were persons in uniform bearing weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it seems that it was quotation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This was quotation -- it seems that it was quotation from his statement given to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. If that was how it was interpreted, that is incorrect. This is the statement that was given to the Defence. This is a 2014 statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was a part of his statement just incorporated in the -- it is a part of his statement given to the Prosecution just incorporated in this statement, and he later commented it as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I -- I think we just had Defence counsel give us some evidence here, Your Honours. I think that was totally inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was just -- just an explanation and you can see the reference. It is 117.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of the paragraph, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I see the footnote, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, this is your 2014 statement that you signed in August of this year; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you -- it was written in the Serbian language; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one was written in Serbian, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And before you signed it, you read through it quite carefully. In fact, we can see from the cover that you spent a number of days putting it together; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I assume that you stand by the statement and what's contained in it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, it was the case that the JNA also considered these prisoners to be prisoners of war, in fact, entitled to the various provisions under international law for the protection of prisoners of war; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I put to you that under the same logic that you have in this letter, this 27 November 1991 letter, the SBWS courts could have exercised subject matter and territorial jurisdiction over Serb perpetrators who committed crimes against civilians in the SBWS; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you properly. My position was that all perpetrators, civilians, who had committed crimes against civilians, were under our jurisdiction. Military officers who committed crimes against civilians or military personnel were under the jurisdiction of the military organs, so I don't see any confusion there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What I'm putting to you is that under the Law on Military Courts, the military courts had jurisdiction over prisoners of war. You stated in your 2014 statement that that's what you knew or believed on the 20th of November, and you've also testified that that was what the JNA considered them to be. In this letter you're seeking to -- you're indicating that you have jurisdiction over those individuals and that the courts in the SBWS should be the ones that try them, and my position to you is that the same could be said about Serbs who may or may not fall within the Law on Military Courts. They also could have been prosecuted within the SBWS for crimes they committed against civilians; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless they were in uniform, members of the TO, and resubordinated to the Army of Yugoslavia. In that case, yes. But that is something that the army had to take care of, the army that arrested them and processed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So you're seeking an exception for prisoners of war but not for Serbs who may wear uniform; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are not asking for an exception. These are just examples of political integral nature and nothing is being done by them. If you wanted to do something, then you would have to have quite specific official documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have P3200 on the screen. This is tab 149.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You were shown this memorandum from Colonel Maksimovic to Colonel Gligorevic concerning your visit to Sremska Mitrovica prison on 10 December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 2 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It is reported that you, Mr. Hadzic, and the other members of this delegation "wanted to inspect the prisoners." Now, you testified during direct examination that it was the JNA representatives who suggested and, indeed, even provoked you into visiting the prisoners. You will agree, Mr. Susa, that nowhere in your 2014 statement or, for that matter, your 2008 statement or Dokmanovic testimony did you make this assertion.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are numerous facts and then additional facts can be tied to those facts. Each of the things that I said could in another half an hour be interpreted by an additional five or six points. None of these processes are simple and they don't take place in a period of a couple of minutes without having a series of conversations and circumstances appearing there, which I cannot recall right away. Everything that I said in my statement that took days and all my testimony before the Tribunal is something that I consider truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In paragraph 125 of your 2014 statement - and you can take a look at that if you'd like - you identify the portions of this particular memorandum that you claim to be untrue.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you repeat the paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: 125. Now, this is -- in this paragraph you identify the portions of this particular memorandum that you claim to be untrue. But as I read it, you make no mention of the report's statement that the delegation, the SBWS delegation, wanted to inspect the prisoners; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The delegation did not want to inspect the prisoners, and what I said actually was much more than what is contained in paragraph 125. I said more than was in that paragraph, but the Defence probably felt that what they have quoted here was enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now during this visit to Sremska Mitrovica, you confronted one of the JNA officers about the fact that the prisoners on the list they provided you were no longer at the KP Dom; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified about that indirectly. I wasn't given any list. I had a report about it from my investigators who were at the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And Mr. Hadzic was present when you were having this confrontation with the JNA representative; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry, I don't know what confrontation the Prosecution refers to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to paragraph 124 of this witness's statement, which I assume the Defence counsel is familiar with, but I don't think it's necessary for the basis of my question. I think I can put this question to the witness regardless of turning to his 2014 statement because in his previous answer he was explaining it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 125 there is no confrontation at all, and I understood that the Prosecution refers to that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No. That -- if that was your understanding, then I apologise. That was not my intention. I'm at this stage not even referring to his statement and I'm proceeding on with my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, you've confirmed about this confrontation that you had regarding the list, and my question simply is that Mr. Hadzic was also present during that confrontation.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that he even heard this conversation. We were sitting in a large room of the hotel, four or five tables were put together. The gentleman that I talked to - I don't know his name - took part in the conversation with me, and I think Mr. Jovan Ajdukovic was there as well, when I warned him about the things that the investigators had warned me about. So I'm not even sure that Goran heard that part of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, it -- now let's do look at your 2014 statement and look at paragraph 124. And if you could look at the bottom third of it, you testify or you put in your statement: "I complained to one of the officers but not to Vujic that people from the list were disappearing from Sremska Mitrovica ..." And then you continue about this discussion. And then at the very end you say: "Goran Hadzic was present during this conversation but did not get involved because it seems that he knew what it was about." Correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. He did not know what it was all about and I said that he didn't know anything about this topic. He was sitting some four or five metres away and he probably didn't hear anything, and I don't think that the topic was something that he was aware of in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So your statement -- your 2014 statement is incorrect in that regard?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My statement on this matter is correct, so I don't know which part you are claiming is incorrect. In this conversation, if you're thinking about the conversation among all of us, there were 10 collocutors. So this conversation that I had with the man was also heard by Jovan Ajdukovic who was sitting next to me. We were talking about facts. Goran Hadzic was not participating in this conversation.
