He was sitting 4 or 5 metres farther away. Perhaps he heard it, perhaps he didn't, but he did not participate in the conversation in any case or know anything about it. Anyway, that is the substance of my statement in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you read to us your last sentence in paragraph 124.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Goran Hadzic was also present during this conversation, but he did not get involved because it seems that he knew nothing about the topic." I repeat, if he heard this conversation, he didn't take part in it. Let's say that he heard it, but he definitely didn't speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, I want to make sure that this is right in the record. Mr. Susa, this last sentence reads: "Goran Hadzic was also present during this conversation, but he did not get involved because ..." Could you read out what is next, "because ..."?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "... because it seems that the topic was not familiar to him."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So then, Mr. Olmsted, there seems to be a translation problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It appears to be, Mr. President. Of course, I can only read the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 3 of this document that's in front of us, this memorandum, regarding your visit. Page 3 of the English, page 2 of the original. Colonel Maksimovic reports that -- that you said that you would bring an armed team to join the work of the JNA investigative team. And then, among other things, the colonel reports that he told you that you would have to discuss this matter with General Vasiljevic. At the time of this meeting, Mr. Susa, on 10 December, no SBWS judges or prosecutors had participated in the operative work at the prison and that is why Mr. -- or Colonel Maksimovic is talking about the future tense, that you have to get permission before the judges come; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. This is definitely not true. It's not true that anybody invoked any armed force that would participate in this. This statement made by the colonel is completely incorrect. The only thing that's true is that our investigating organs were already involved. They had already received permission to do that from the commander of the 1st Military District. They did not ask Colonel Maksimovic's permission for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: As Colonel Maksimovic advised you, you and Mr. Hadzic met with General Vasiljevic at Sremska Mitrovica prison a few days later; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not meet with General Vasiljevic. I don't know whether Goran Hadzic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, after your 10 December visit to Sremska Mitrovica prison, did you write any correspondence to the JNA, to the SFRY Presidency, or to the Republic of Serbia regarding these Croat prisoners held at this prison?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before our first visit to Sremska Mitrovica, to the KP Dom, I wrote exclusively to the commander of the 1st Military District who allowed the operative officers to come into the KPD. After that, I didn't write anything to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So you never wrote to the JNA leadership regarding the horrible conditions you saw at the prison, did you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not deal with it later and I didn't speak about that. The conditions were not horrible. They were bad. They could have been better.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I'll suggest that during your testimony you used much stronger terms. But my question to you is that you didn't feel compelled to write to the 1st Military District about the horrible conditions you -- you saw there or, as you now put it, the mildly bad conditions that you saw there?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I'm using milder terms now. Let's go back to the word "horrible." To me, all conditions where people are detained are horrible. What I was thinking was that the issue of these POWs would be dealt by the ICRC. I did not have this under my control and I didn't think that I am supposed to write any more about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Mr. Susa, I put to you that the information contained in this memorandum is, in fact, accurate, and that the testimony that you provided during direct examination and just now was crafted by you to avoid responsibility for what you and Mr. Hadzic said and did during this visit to the prison?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of that visit to the jail, we didn't do anything. What I said before this honourable Court is true and I stand by it. The bulk of this gentleman's report does not reflect real facts and events.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, the evidence presented in this case so far shows that in addition to being the first and only Serb charged with war crimes by the SBWS and RSK courts, Dusan Boljevic was also the only Serb tried before the SBWS and RSK courts for a serious crime committed against non-Serbs in 1991. That was the case, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you I don't have the exact information about that. I'm not even supposed to have it. Leaders of various bodies should have that information, such as the higher district court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So as minister of justice, you didn't believe it was important to know whether crimes committed against non-Serbs in 1991 during the course of the conflict were investigated and being prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to remind you that the affairs dealt with by the Ministry of Justice are clearly prescribed. It was not our job to get involved in investigating procedures. Any interference in that would have been considered abuse of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's bring up 65 ter 6566. This is tab 159.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is a 9 November 1992 letter from the Knin District Court to the RSK minister of interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could just flip quickly to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that you, the minister of justice, was -- were sent a copy of this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if we go back to page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a letter from Judge Kresovic, and he writes that: "The Court is investigating Cedo Budisavljevic and four other members of the police station in Teslingrad for the murder of Mane Rakic, his two sons and daughter, and the disposal of their bodies in a pit called Golubnjaca in Sracko Selo [phoen], in October 1991." Now, first of all, the perpetrators and victims of this crime were all Serb; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if we stay on page 1 of the original and turn to page 2 of the English version, Kresovic also writes that when the investigation team checked the pit containing the Rakic family, they discovered that it had served during this war as a dumping ground for another 40 bodies of the citizens of the Croatian nationality. And he reports that he provided this information to the president of the RSK Supreme Court and RSK justice minister about this discovery. Kresovic then asserts: "The issue on hand is how to pull out and identify the bodies of the Rakic family without pulling out and identifying other bodies? Do we take out all the bodies found in the pit? What to do so that the UNPROFOR doesn't learn about the pit and all those bodies that it contains, and what if UNPROFOR does find out and demands to take out all the bodies from the pit? How to justify all that in front of the domestic and international public?" He then asks for a concrete stand on this, which he calls "problem of a political nature." Mr. Susa, it was the policy of the RSK government to not investigate crimes against non-Serbs that occurred before the arrival of UNPROFOR, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the policy of this government was. My policy was to continue working on this, and that perhaps marks the beginning of my conflict with certain persons in this region. I gave my full support to Judge Kresovic and his intention to proceed with this because it's obvious that he had already begun.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Those 40 Croat victims, they were never investigated by RSK authorities, were they?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authorities of the RSK were not supposed to carry out this investigation. It was the district court in Knin, headed by Mr. Kresovic. I don't know why he failed to carry out this investigation, if he did, and I don't know who stopped him from carrying it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll admit this into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 6566 will be Exhibit P3285.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, in addition to prosecuting non-Serbs for war crimes, crimes of genocide, et cetera, it was also the priority of the SBWS and RSK governments to prosecute non-Serbs for crimes against the state under chapter 15 of the SFRY criminal code; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of the things they handled. I would not say it was a priority. And it was not an affair of the government but the courts. The government had no powers to prosecute anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So the government did not at all interfere with the judicial determination as to whether to prosecute non-Serbs for armed rebellion and other chapter 15 crimes. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. The government could not meddle in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we see 1D1022. This is tab 238.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Well, the document can be pulled up. But before you continue, Mr. Olmsted, one moment. Mr. Susa, you said that: "The authorities of the RSK were not supposed to carry out this investigation. It was the district court in Knin ..." Could you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The judiciary has sole jurisdiction over courts. The government cannot decide on opening investigations and starting trials and the way how these trials would end. The government cannot interfere with this. The Assembly assigned all competencies in this area to courts and their bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I'll ask for the moment. Please continue, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have in front of us is a 9 March 1992 mandatory work directive from you to the RSK judiciary. Now, I believe it was yesterday or the day before where Defence counsel showed you an earlier mandatory work directive that you issued regarding the transfer of property. As minister of justice, you issued these mandatory directives from time to time, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to do that in general, not in specific individual cases. I could not decide how people should proceed in a specific case, but regarding a certain occurrence or phenomenon, I could state my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, it's more than your opinion. This is a mandatory work directive. And the one we looked at yesterday or the day before was also a mandatory work directive. But let's look at what this one says. You observe: "By analysing the structure of recent crimes, we have noticed that the share of investigations, indictments, and criminal proceedings against persons who have taken part in any way in organising or directly carrying out the armed rebellion against the state of SFRY or the Republic of Serbian Krajina is negligible." You then instruct the public prosecutor's offices to immediately initiate co-ordination committee or co-ordination meetings with the police and request the "accelerated gathering of evidence against all persons for whom there are reasonable grounds to suspect that they have perpetrated or are still perpetrating crimes prescribed under Chapters 15 and 16 of the SFRY Criminal Code." Mr. Susa, this directive conveys the position not only of you but also the RSK government; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that first of all it reflects my communications with the judiciary. If this were transmitting directly the position of the government, then this document would be signed -- we were not yet fully established at that moment. It would have been signed by Zdravko Zecevic. As to your question whether this was an important area of work for our organs, this concerns the gravest forms of very serious crimes. Of course, this was very well represented in the work of the judiciary and it was important for us to deal with it. If you think that it was more important to deal with civil lawsuits at that time, I must say I don't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mention that the RSK government had not been fully formed by March 1992. Was this the position then of the SBWS government? You are, after all, issuing it as minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time I was no longer a member of the SBWS -- no, no. Sorry. At this time I was already a member of the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. I can't see well whether it's March or some other month. In February 1992, a part of the RSK government was formed. Not all ministries were in place yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D1022 will be Exhibit P3286.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could have on the screen now 1D1020. This is tab 236.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, what we have in front of us is a 7 April 1992 memorandum from the Republican Prosecutor Milorad Trosic to the RSK Supreme Court. And if you can look at the first couple of paragraphs, you can see that Mr. Trosic is writing with regard to your mandatory directive and reports that the Vukovar SUP has so far compiled a large number of criminal reports against about 2.000 Ustasha in absentia. A month after your directive, the judiciary and the police had compiled a substantial number of cases against non-Serbs, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say that it happened after -- a month after my dispatch. This is combined information at the time when this was written. The process of collecting information about crimes against Serbs had by that time lasted for a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I'm a little bit confused by your last answer. As I understand it, the SBWS courts came into existence or began to function at the beginning of November 1991. This is dated five months later. So these reports were gathered or investigated and submitted within those five months; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not talking now about the investigations conducted by courts. I was talking about the documentation available on crimes that were perpetrated, and police bodies and other bodies and organisations had been working on it for more than a year.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were investigating murders, arsons, and other crimes. The courts did not pursue all this all at the same time. On that date in April 1992, the number of these investigations and cases was about 2.000. And let me add: Based on all the information that we have here, only a small number was found to be relevant and was pursued by issuing indictments.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: He then notes that the processing of these criminal reports is a huge task. That's correct, isn't it? That this kind of activity, investigating and filing criminal reports against Ustasha, in absentia, was a tremendous amount of work. It required a lot of judicial resources.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was to be done seriously, establishing facts, then it was a very serious job and that's how we treated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Trosic next raises the issue that your directive was not a sufficient guarantee that the RSK courts will conduct criminal proceedings against Ustasha for crimes pursuant to chapters 15 and 16, noting that: "They are crimes which are strictly within the jurisdiction of the military judiciary." Mr. Susa, that's a correct interpretation of Article 13 of the SFRY Law on Military Courts, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm glad to know that my organs know the regulations very well and interpret them properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Trosic then requests the supreme court to provide its opinion on whether the RSK courts can conduct criminal proceedings against Ustasha for chapters 15 and 16 crimes as soon as possible. "Considering that criminal proceedings against the majority of Ustasha who are beyond our reach now should commence before the arrival of UN forces." The goal was to complete the processing of non-Serbs for chapters 15 and 16 crimes before the UN arrived, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the goal was. I did not take part in this communication between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The RSK authorities knew that the UN forces would perceive these kinds of criminal proceedings as a veiled attempt to prevent non-Serbs from returning under the Vance Plan, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are making a drastic and rough mistake which I need to point out to you. You neglect the fact that there was a large number of victims. You are dealing here with numbers of potential perpetrators that we are not sure of. At no point in time do you introduce the category that is important to me, and that is the number of casualties. So please, because of them and because of their families, this is something that we really do need to take into account. We did not have 2.000 people in our hands so that the UN would free them. Why would we be bothered about the arrival of the UN in this case? You need to ask Trosic about this. I would have been glad to have seen the UN and to have shown them the number of the missing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, if you could repeat your last sentence. The interpreters missed it.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have liked for the UN forces to have taken part in all of this, to have reviewed all the facts that we had at our disposal, and to have assisted and helped us to have all the perpetrators before the face of justice regardless of whether they would have been tried in Croatia or before military courts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Mr. Susa, I don't know if you heard from the interpreters, but if you could please slow down so that they can catch everything that you say.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Under chapter 15 of the SFRY criminal code, which covers crimes against the state, which is referenced in your directive as well as Mr. Trosic's memo to the supreme court, those crimes include things such as Article 119, service in the enemy armed forces; Article 124, which is armed rebellion; and Article 136, creating a joint enterprise for the purpose of hostile activities. These sorts of crimes, the victim is not persons lying in grave-sites. It's the state, isn't it? It's either the RSK or the FRY; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand the interpreter. What does it have to do with all of this, how many people are lying in grave-sites? Perhaps the interpreter did not understand what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your last answer was with regard to the victims, which I appreciate. But what I am asking you about is under chapter 15 of the SFRY criminal code, crimes against the state, in those crimes the victim is not persons but rather it's the state itself. In this case, it was the RSK; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are now putting me in the position of commenting on the position of the Republican Prosecutor, Milorad Trosic. I cannot do that at this point. And I do not know what he meant to when he referred to chapters 15 and 16 of the SFRY. I really don't know at this point if I could comment on something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't just Mr. Trosic who brought up chapter 15. You did in your mandatory directive which we looked at a moment ago, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is so, then we have a position which is very simple. This is not then a question of the most serious crimes but crimes against the armed forces, against the order of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. That is the same principle that we apparently applied in relation to each other. At that point in time in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, there was a large number of cases like this that was being conducted. Perhaps I don't remember that. All of this was some kind of reciprocity.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D1020 will be Exhibit P3287.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to complete the picture, if we could 1D1021 on the screen. This is tab 237.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have before us is a 14 April 1992 memorandum from the president of the RSK Supreme Court to the republican prosecutor's office. And we can see that Mr. Vojnovic responds to Mr. Trosic's memorandum from a week earlier authorising the prosecutor's office to start proceedings Chapters 15 and 16 criminal reports until final resolution of the issues as agreed with the assistant minister of justice on 9 April this year. Which assistant minister is Mr. Vojnovic referring to?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that was Mr. Lukovic at that point. I'm not sure but I think that it was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Consistent with your mandatory directive and the supreme court's decision that we are looking at, criminal proceedings were initiated against tens of thousands of non-Serbs for chapter 15, crimes against the state; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the number that you have just mentioned. We did not have the documents for so many people or even paper. I don't know how many people this particular investigation encompasses. I don't know where you got this information from.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, we'll come back to that perhaps, Mr. Susa.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D1021 will be Exhibit P3288.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: By way of just a few examples of these chapter 15 cases, may we have on the screen 65 ter 6668. This is tab 161.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a 5 February 1992 criminal report.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps we can zoom in a little bit on the original version. It's a little bit dark. The date is obviously on the upper left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we see the name of the first accused, who is identified as a Croat, and then it proceeds to list a number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 3 of the English, page 12 of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that the number of accused non-Serbs is 173. And then we can see from the paragraph that follows the listing of the perpetrators, that these non-Serbs are charged with committing the crime of association for hostile purposes against the Serb nation in 1990 to 1991 under Article 136 of the SFRY criminal code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't see where it is stated that they were accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, they were charged, let's say. This is a criminal report and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a charging document, Your Honours. If I misspoke --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I -- I think that they have the status of suspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Certainly. Innocent until proven guilty. And by the way, by no means do I or the Prosecution represent that these charges were properly filed, and that they had a basis for charging these non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But let's look at the charges as is reported here at the end of this charging document, they are charged with Article 136 under Chapter 15 of the SFRY criminal code. This is consistent with your mandatory directive as well as with the supreme court's memo to Mr. Trosic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are completely in the wrong. What you are showing me is a criminal report of the Secretariat for Internal Affairs. This is the police. We do not have to act pursuant to these reports unless there is sufficient evidence on the existence of reasonable grounds. You can have 150.000 people on such a criminal report, but that does not mean anything to the court. It depends. I would need to know whether criminal charges were actually filed and criminal proceedings initiated on the basis of this report, but I am not the minister of the interior. This is something that I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: My question to you is that it is consistent with your directive which stated that these cases, these types of cases, should be investigated, and in fact, I'll quote from it, your directive. It says: "In connection with the above and in addition to carrying out activities related to the submitting of criminal reports, conducting proceedings against suspects and passing judgements," et cetera, et cetera. This is a criminal report that's consistent with what you were seeking in your directive; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report cannot be submitted on the basis of my directive because this organ is not familiar with the content of my directive. Precisely because of the fact that there was a large number of such reports, we were snowed under, and I was being asked to start considering them. So in a way, I encouraged the prosecutor's offices and the courts to look into what is happening here. I did not encourage the police to submit such a large number of criminal reports. Or if there were really elements for suspicion, they needed to submit them in the same or an even greater number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I see the time, Your Honours. Just one question before I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: -- lose the stream.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You said that you were asked to look into this matter. Who asked you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The organs of internal affairs who were telling us that they were delivering a large number of criminal reports that we were not beginning to work on. In principle that was true, but we were in a position to think about all of these things in a slightly different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We will take the second break or it is -- yeah, the second break, of course, 30 minutes. We will be back at 12.45. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness enters the courtroom, I found the one error in either in translation or in the transcription.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At page 52, line 16 and 17, he stated that -- it states: "The government assigned all competencies in this area to courts and their bodies." He didn't say "the government" but "assembly."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm wondering if it would be better if the Defence simply submits a request for a translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think, indeed, that would be -- that would -- or verification of the audio. That would be indeed appropriate, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, let's ask how -- what is your planning for the cross? How long will you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm going to use the full amount of time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You intend to need to use the full amount. Okay. Five minutes before 2.00 you should interrupt then, because the Defence wants to raise an administrative matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, I want to show you just a couple more of these criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can take a look at 65 ter 6669. It's tab 162.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can maybe zoom in a little bit on the original because it is a bit dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is just, Mr. Susa, another criminal report. This one from 10 February 1992. And it's of similar nature to the last one we looked at. We can see that the first suspect charged in this criminal report is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could just go to page 6 in the English, page 13 of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We can see that the report is against 176 suspects, and the paragraphs that follow the list of names indicates that this is another example of non-Serbs being charged under Article 136 of Chapter 15 of the SFRY criminal code for association for hostile purposes in 1990, 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, even though the document is hardly legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could look at one more of these. It's 65 ter 6674. This is tab 164. And just zoom in a little bit on the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We can see that this is a 5 May 1992 criminal report against, again we can see from the first names, Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 3 of the English, 100 of the original. Yes, and I think if we can turn to the next page in the English. I'm sorry, if we could just advance one page in the English. Let's see. There we go. Now we're on the right page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that this one is against 1.432 suspects, and we can see from the text that follows that this is another example of non-Serbs being charged under Article 136 for association for hostile purposes in 1990, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we zoom maybe a bit into the original. I think the first paragraph will suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Susa?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. I don't see anything, but I think it's all right. I think they're all in the same -- I think they're all drafted in the same context. I think that it's quite dark, the text, so I don't know that there would be any problem if we zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, we could try zooming in a little bit. I'm interested in the first paragraph. I think it indicates that it's under Article 136 on the third line.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Maybe we could zoom in on Article 136.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Susa, can you see that its charging in Article 136 -- oh, there we go. 136. There we go.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it. 136, paragraph 1, item 1, and then Article 24, paragraph 1, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we tender into evidence 6668, 6669, and 6674.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They will be assigned Exhibit Numbers P3289, P2 -- pardon me, P3290, and P3291, respectively. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, I have one more document in this same vein that may be a little bit difficult to read but we'll try our luck.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 6698. This is tab 294. And you'll need to zoom in on the original.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There is no translation for this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. We'll come back to that, then. It's been released now, Your Honours. In the meantime, perhaps while it's being released, we could zoom in on the original just so that the witness has an opportunity to take a closer look at it. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, what we have in front of us are -- this is the first of three 20 December 1993 rulings releasing Croat detainees indicted or convicted of serving an enemy army, and they are being released for prisoner exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can scroll down a little bit on the original, and if we could turn to the next page. Zoom in on the original. And if we could just turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see the -- by the way, that the prisoner exchange occurred on the 28th of -- well, I stand corrected. That an agreement on prisoner exchange was reached on the 28th of November, 1993, in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We can turn to the next page in the original just to show the second one of this. And zoom in on the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that this is also a 20 December 1993 ruling ending custody of a Croat charged with serving in the enemy army. And I know it's a little bit hard to read, Mr. Susa, at least in the original, but it pertains to this prisoner exchange that was arranged. And my question to you is: That was the situation, wasn't it, Mr. Susa, that non-Serbs who were convicted of Chapter 15 crimes, such as serving in an enemy army, they were -- after they were detained and prosecuted and served a sentence for a while, many were subject to prisoner exchange; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I can't really make out this text, but let's say it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's turn to the first page of this document. And zoom in to the bottom half of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps now you can see that this is a release from detention for the purposes of a prisoner exchange.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Prosecutor, let's go ahead. I could spend another futile hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll just note that this first ruling in the second -- or, actually, it's the third paragraph indicates that this person was indicted on the 17th of March, 1993, for crimes under Chapter 15 of the SFRY criminal code.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Based on the fact that that indictment occurred in 1993, would you like to revise your testimony that the criminal code of the FRY did not apply to the RSK in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the creation of a joint state, this law could be used only in the absence of regulations that we still didn't have. If at this moment the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was already formed consisting only of Serbia and Montenegro and we had no other piece of legislation for this area, then we had to use this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P3292.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, you were aware that members of the RSK police were participating in crimes against the remaining non-Serb population in 1992 and 1993, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this was covered by criminal reports in all the other cases, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at P2847. This is tab 287.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what I'm about to show you is a United Nations report dated 27 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I would like to turn to page 5 of the original, page 4 of the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I want to draw your attention paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could zoom in on that a bit in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that this is a Secretary-General report to the United Nations, and he reports that non-Serbs with property were being targeted for expulsion through threats and other acts of intimidation and that the property they left behind was looted, demolished, or occupied. He then reports that UNCIVPOL monitors have received reports that police or "milicija" involvement directly or indirectly in these incidents. Mr. Susa, that was the situation in the SBWS, as well throughout the RSK, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a typical situation. It would be very important for me to see the names of possible perpetrators here. And there is a contradiction here: Nobody could be moved into torched houses or destroyed houses. Such cases were in the smallest minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at P1957.1. This is tab 88.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what I'm about to show you is a 12 October 1992 Official Note by DB Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 3 of the English, page 4 of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that the note discusses an RSK Assembly session held in Vukovar on the 28th of September, 1992, at which many questions were asked concerning the work of the police and the judicial system over which you and Milan Martic were called to account. And it goes on to state that the fiercest attacks were by Eastern Slovenian Assemblymen against Martic "concerning the illegal conduct of the police which was accused of looting and other crimes." First of all, do you recall this debate at the RSK Assembly session in September 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember the details. I know that people were called out because of failures in the Ministry of the Interior and also our work, wherein I managed to explain what problems we were facing and there occurred a conflict between us and the Ministry of Defence. We were just called out. There were no attacks. I believe it was Martic who was attacked. When I was called out as responsible for some failures, I think I managed to make our case well. But he also had to explain the failures in the work of the Ministry of the Interior, Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And those failures included crimes being committed by the RSK police, and in particular, they were committing crimes against the non-Serb population that remained in the RSK, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This assembly session did not discuss that in these terms. I accused the Ministry of the Interior and Martic more because of the shortcomings in their work. I didn't have any particular information that I could attach to a particular person and accuse him or her. I cannot accept such generalised assessments, because I cannot find that one single person was responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned failures on the part of the police. The police were failing to report crimes committed against the non-Serb population, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I repeat that I have no precise information about that. I didn't know about a particular case that I could lay at their door. I knew that their criminal reports were sloppily done, that records of events were -- or incidents were not properly done, and we could not proceed on the basis of them, and that they did not follow the law strictly in putting people and keeping them in custody. That's all I could do. I didn't know of any particular offence committed by a member of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let us look at 1D2991. This is tab 271. And this is the report on the work of the Ministry of Justice and administration for the period between 28 May 1992 and 1 March 1993. If we could just turn to page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is your report, isn't it, Mr. Susa?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 3 in both the English and the original. I think if maybe perhaps we can move to the earlier page in the English version. All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now in this report you write: "In certain areas, such as Vukovar, the judicial organs have not always had real co-operation with the organs of the interior. The judicial organs are being told that the police would not be a service for the courts or the prosecutor's offices in that area." You then further note: "Reports are not being filed and known perpetrators of crimes are not arrested because they are the 'great liberators.'" That was a real problem in 1992 and 1993, Mr. Susa, wasn't it? And not just in the SBWS but throughout the RSK.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that was a problem everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And one person who was considered to be a great liberator was Slobodan Jurisic, which I believe you mention in your 2014 statement.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the person who committed crimes and we prosecuted him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, he was accused of the murder of two Croat members of the Alicic family -- or, I'm sorry, the Alic family, back in February 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I can't be sure about the date. I believe that the last name Alic is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the case never made it to trial in the RSK, did it? In fact, it was only in 2000 that the Belgrade District Court, under a separate indictment, convicted Jurisic; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's true. We conducted proceedings against Jurisic. I don't have any information about that now, but I believe proceedings were taken in our territory. I believe Jurisic escaped and then he was later recaptured in Serbia, but I know eventually he was convicted of this crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let us look at 1D102 -- I'm sorry, 1D1086. This is tab 250. And if we could zoom in on the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a petition for the release of our comrade and friend Slobodan Jurisic, and the petition states: "We should not allow resistance fighters, such honourable and decent people like Slobodan Jurisic, to be in prison, to be charged with things he did not do, to have a staged trial, which could then be the basis for trials against some other resistance fighters too." And then the petition ends by demanding the release of Jurisic. This is an example, Mr. Susa, isn't it of the attitude towards great liberators that was demonstrated by the police throughout the RSK; isn't it correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you've drawn the wrong conclusion. This is a petition by a certain number of people. It's not a petition from the police force. I would not infer from this that the police was not doing its job. I think that somebody was bothered by the fact that this man was in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Because he was considered a great liberator; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know this man, Jurisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If you can look at the sixth signature on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Scroll a little bit over to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really see.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we zoom in to the sixth signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whose signature is it. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, that's Goran Hadzic's signature, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I allow that it's possible. I don't know his signature, but I allow the possibility. If he said it himself and confirmed it and you are repeating it to me now, I'm not going to dispute it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm putting it to you, Mr. Susa, and you would be familiar with his signature having worked for him for a number of years.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just because I worked with him I don't necessarily know his signature. I've seen so many signatures. I cannot recognise a signature in this form unless it is also typewritten. And this is pretty illegible. I can recognise some of the signatures. In fact, I can make out what is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us who else signed this document of people you know?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I know Vladimir Nudic [phoen]. That's the brother of Goran's wife. These are all people from Vukovar. I don't know them, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we tender into evidence 1D2991, which was the previous document, and 1D1086.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They should be assigned Exhibit Numbers P3293 and P3294, respectively. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The judiciary was also susceptible to political influence, wasn't it? And I'm talking about the 1992, 1993 period in particular.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was pressure, but not influence. It was hard enough to work under pressure, but we were not influenced in our judgements by politicians. I always supported all the personnel of the courts and I congratulated them on their persistence and their high principles in abiding by the law. But pressure, yes, there was pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that pressure also manifested itself in the appointment of judges and prosecutors; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To what extent? What do you mean? What kind of pressure in making appointments?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's look at an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have P3081 on the screen. This is tab 81.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what I'm about to show you is the transcript from the 20 April 1993 RSK Assembly session. I think you looked at a bit of that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 10 of the original, page 15 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We can see that you are speaking, Mr. Susa, and you proposed the election of a number of judges. And included on this list --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page -- oh, it's still on this page. Page 10 of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Josip Nikolajevic. I pronounced his name probably incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Djuro Pavlica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 18 of the English, page 11 of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that one of the assembly members present at the session stated that he could not accept the proposal of Josip Nikolajevic, an ethnic Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the next page on the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You responded that: Nikolajevic authorised texts that spoke affirmatively of our whole struggle.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I believe we could stay on the same page here for the original, but if we could turn to page 19 for the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The assembly member then responded: "I simply would not allow for a Croat to be administering judgement in this situation and there can be no question about this either."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if we can turn to page 13 of the original, page 21 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that you say, towards the bottom, I believe: "As far as Mr. Nikolajevic is concerned, I can't judge on that matter. However, please let it not be the definitive and principled position that people who are not of Serb ethnicity cannot work in the judiciary. It wouldn't be good. There are some among us who may have been a better choice. Perhaps they still are and they are Serbs and Hungarians. It wouldn't be good for there to be any sort of connotation from which one could perceive that we would be going with eliminating such people." Now, as the government's attorney, you were concerned about the international perception of rejecting a judicial candidate because of his ethnicity; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my entire work from the beginning until this thing that you just quoted, I defended my positions and I'm still proud of them and proud of my work as a lawyer and counsel. I was not a judicial candidate because we never had that position. I always advocated the admission of qualified and professional cadres even when that was not easy. And I can confirm that before this Court. It was not easy. Many people couldn't accept it because they were victimised by various things in the war, but finally I managed to push this through. I was not afraid of any international forces here. This reflects my personal approach to this whole problem and my world view.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, as a solution, you recommended they come up with a better qualified Serb or Hungarian; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I said here was that there were people who were perhaps better than we are and that we need to think about that regardless of whether they were Croats or Hungarians, perhaps. And then in spite of that, already at the next assembly Mr. Nikolajevic was elected judge. I don't see that part of the text, but I know what I was thinking at the time. In the context of everything that I said. It's not that I was praising Serbs. Some people here think that Serbs are, by the very virtue of being Serbs, the best. Unfortunately, here that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, the transcript, Mr. Susa, reads -- I guess it's at the very bottom of the original, you stated: "... it wouldn't be good. There are some among us who may have been a better choice ..." And I think we have to turn to the next page. And you continue: "... perhaps they still are and they are Serbs and Hungarians." And then you make the statement that it would not be good for there to be any sort of connotation. That's what you said, isn't it, Mr. Susa?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there -- this has been badly written by the minute-keeper. I'm not thinking of Serbs and Hungarians. I'm thinking of the elimination of people such as Nikolajevic. I did not believe in any context that it would be good to believe that we would be going for the elimination of such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 14 of the original, page 21 of the English. And again, page 21 of the English; page 14 of the original. Good. Oh, it's ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: These are the exact pages you called.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. Then I stand corrected. Is this page 21 of the English, though? It is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is e-court page 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, maybe I have the wrong page. Oh, yes, it's at the bottom of the English page, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: With regard to Djuro Pavlica, another candidate for judge, an assembly member raised the issue that: "This judicial candidate had tried cases against about a dozen Lapac Serbs, it is known what for, at the beginning of our struggle for the Krajina and for the Serb people." Mr. Susa, can you tell us what were those dozen Serbs from Lapac tried for?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably for two reasons: By the Croatian military judicial organs, they were arrested for rebellion --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't there as a lawyer, but I know more or less what was happening from the press.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, the interpreters asked the witness to repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, could you repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will repeat my answer. I'm sorry. Many people, including these Serbs from Lapac, were prosecuted in Croatia parallel on two tracks by the Croatian military judicial organs, prosecuted them all, thousands of other peoples, for armed rebellion. And then other than that, the civilian Croatian judiciary prosecuted us for dismantling of the Croatian constitutional order. This applied also in the case of these Serbs from Lapac and all the other Serbs from the area of Krajina, the Serbian regions, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 24 of the English, page 16 of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, I'll put to you that at the end of this debate regarding these two nominees, the assembly voted against those appointments. And in fact, they weren't made judges; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know about Mr. Pavlica. I think that he moved to a different job later. As for Mr. Nikolajevic, he was denied the right to try cases at this assembly but at the next assembly he passed through. I wanted to affirm the humanity and the professional value of these people, and for me nothing here was controversial. The essence was that I could not appoint or replace anybody as a judge of my own initiative. This was something that the assembly was to do. And in this case, the assembly, under the influence of certain people or groups, could not accept my proposal. But for the next assembly session, I managed to prepare well. I prepared better. It's also possible that the tensions were reduced that time, but anyway it all went well in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 6689 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, you had an opportunity to look at this document during proofing? It was on the Defence's exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, this is a wartime job classification in the RSK Ministry of Justice and judicial body. So it contains a list of all the officials and employees of both the Ministry of Justice as well as the judiciary and prosecution office; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it should be. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this report is dated March 1994 but it generally reflects the positions that existed in the RSK Ministry of Justice and judiciary at the end of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that. I did not work on any kind of wartime classification. This was done by the gentleman who came after me as minister of justice, so that the situation at the end of 1993 and during this period does not have to be the same. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, with the exception of a few possible Hungarians, the officials listed in this document are all Serbs, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was inevitable because the Croatians had left the area. It's not that they were there and we did not want to elect them. Everybody who was there, somebody at one assembly session or another assembly session, on my assistance, having informed them about it, they began to start to work at the job that they were good at. It's not that they were not being appointed. It's just that they simply weren't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And having looked through this document, I don't find the name of Nikolajevic on this list. Did you find his name on this list?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't look for it. Believe me. I know that Nikolajevic worked in the court. Perhaps he was not a judge, he was perhaps a professional associate. But at one point he became a judge. He did remain in the court where he continued to work. I don't know if he worked as a judge or perhaps he remained there working as a professional associate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you name any other Croat judges who were employed back in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say. I think that there were some, but I didn't particularly meet either Serbs or Croats. They were all the same to me. And if they were doing their job properly, I had full respect for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P3295.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You've testified about your role in abolishing the military courts in 1993. Now, you proposed the abolition of those military courts because forming them usurped Mr. Hadzic's power as president; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Obviously you didn't understand that properly. There is no power involved there. First of all, military courts were never formed as independent organs because we didn't have a sufficient number of cadres. The RSK constitution gave the right to Mr. Hadzic to appoint in wartime circumstances judges, prosecutors, and others judicial organs. This did not have anything to do with his later competencies. The problem was created because at the time of the forming of the organs and the need to form the organs, nobody consulted Mr. Hadzic. The consultation and the elections were carried out at the level of the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of the Interior. Even the justice minister and administration was not consulted even though the largest part of the cadres were pulled out from his bodies. Another bad thing was that in the work of the military judicial organs formed in this way, you also had some laypersons working there. For me, as far as I was concerned, this was something that was impermissible and it was dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And Mr. Hadzic shared your views regarding the abolition of these military courts that were formed; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I repeat, he agreed only with the indisputable fact that the then election was a violation of the constitution, but we had to say something because that would have drawn us into a whole series of legal violations. And then once that snowballed, you would be in a position where you couldn't correct these matters anymore. The competencies that Mr. Hadzic had were not something that he took upon himself but was granted by the assembly. Once he was granted them, he had to exercise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 6690. This is tab 178.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a petition from representatives of Banija and Kordun dated 1 March 1993. And if you could turn -- if you just look at the beginning of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And then we'll turn to page 2 in both the English and the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In the petition, the representatives advocate keeping the military court in their area because the court was stamping out smuggling and other crimes and the court was found great -- had found great approval among the people. Now, first of all, the military courts that were, according to you, being established illegally or against the constitution, those courts were located in SAO Krajina; in particular, in Banija and Kordun, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To military courts or military courts. It seems that they did begin to operate here. And later I can tell you why that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Right now all I'm interested in knowing is that these military courts that you had an issue with, they were in SAO Krajina, weren't they? They were not in SBWS.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did not exist in the SBWS. I said in the SAO Krajina only and that only in the region of Banija and Kordun.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And it's correct that the municipal or village authorities wanted these courts, these military courts to function because they were stamping out smuggling and other economic crimes committed in their areas; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what would you say if I were to tell you that it was actually quite the opposite. If you look at the previous session that we have just analysed what the conduct was of deputy Milos Vukcevic and who is a good judge as far as he's concerned? Only those that he knew. You can compare these two things and then see why this is only happening in Banija and Kordun, because these presidents of municipalities were involved in a very, very good venture that involved smuggling from the Cazin Krajina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down and to repeat the last sentence of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, could you repeat your last sentence.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The judges that they knew in the field suited them. They were all those from their areas that they knew very well and nobody was complaining about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P3296. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter 6693. This is tab 181.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have in front of us is a 9 June 1993 dispatch from Milan Martic to all RSK SUPs and SJBs, and Martic is reporting on decisions adopted by the RSK Supreme Defence Council. Mr. Susa, that was the council over which Mr. Hadzic presided over as RSK president once it was formed in 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did preside over it and he was in the classic position of primus inter pares, first among equals, and the decisions had to be adopted by consensus. Yes, in a formal sense he did preside over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can look at item 4, we see that it states that summary proceedings for discharging fire-arms will be conducted by civilian courts as agreed with the Ministry of Justice. This is an example of the Supreme Defence Council implementing Mr. Hadzic's presidential decrees giving the civilian courts jurisdiction over crimes; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Goran Hadzic could not change the jurisdiction of civilian courts. All he could do in wartime conditions was to form military courts. Here we are remaining on the matter that I spoke about, that civilian and local courts can decide about everything. There was no need to form any military courts, and then they here say the civilian courts will conduct the proceedings according to military rules.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Please slow down, Mr. Susa, because the interpreters do need time to interpret what you're saying. In January -- late January 1993, and in early February 1993, Mr. Hadzic used his wartime powers to pass a number of decrees and included in those decrees was a decree that gave the civilian courts jurisdiction over military cases; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this happened in this case, that would be the legal way, the legal form. I cannot testify to this because I think that, in this case, I was no longer the justice and administration minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P3297. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, Goran Hadzic never exercised his presidential powers to establish military courts and prosecutors' offices in the RSK, did he?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not, but others acted in his name without his authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that's what I -- what I was asking, that Mr. Hadzic never established military courts in the RSK while he was president; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Olmsted. Thank you. Mr. Susa, this is the end of the hearings this week. You will have to come back on Monday at 9.00. I remind you that you are still a witness, that you stay under oath, and that you cannot communicate with either party or discuss your testimony with anybody. Thank you. The court usher will escort you out of court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Court adjourned.
